items.title: Bill Holman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999
items.q: a lot of people left, Bob Cooper and Bud Shank and Shelly Manne and Shorty Rogers, a lot of the stars left

ctx.x: Were you on the band when he had the — didn’t he have a string section for a while?

Yeah. I think they called that the “Innovations in Modern Jazz” or something, so they called it the Innovations Orchestra. That was, he did two tours with that, I think in ’48 and ’49. That was before me. Then in 1951, at the end of 1951, a lot of people left, Bob Cooper and Bud Shank and Shelly Manne and Shorty Rogers, a lot of the stars left. So when he reorganized the band in early ’52 that’s when I joined. But no strings.
He certainly generates discussion about where he fits in jazz history. How do you feel about his place?

items.title: Holman Bill — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Bud Shank had a working group here toward the end

ctx.x: People talk about L.A. in that regard every once in a while. It seems to boil down to that there‟s too much to do here. But there‟s an inertia among the people here.

They don‟t go out at night like in New York, where you can see a jazz club filled on a weeknight. You don‟t see anybody around here on a weeknight. There were a few clubs here. Bud Shank had a working group here toward the end – toward the late – when Mel and I had our group, Bud had a group working them. Buddy Collette had a group. In fact, Gerald Wilson was playing trumpet with him in a quintet. It was hard to find gigs at that time, but there were some around. Yeah, there was a few groups playing, but they…

There was a significant – you said there were some clubs. The one that comes immediately to mind is the Lighthouse, which got a lot of attention, got a lot of press, and figures prominently in the history of jazz on the West Coast. Can you talk about that venue and the scene there?
